subject: math
title: Data and Graphs: Stem-and-Leaf Plots, Multiple-Bar Graphs, Mean, Median and Mode
seo_title: Grade 4 Data and Graphs Worksheets: Stem-and-Leaf Plots, Mean, Median, Mode (Free, Answer Key, Ontario)
standard_text: Determine the mean and the median and identify the mode(s), if any, for various data sets involving whole numbers, and explain what each of these measures indicates about the data
meta_desc: Free Grade 4 math worksheets on data and graphs for the Ontario curriculum: qualitative and quantitative data, frequency tables, stem-and-leaf plots, multiple-bar graphs, the mean as a fair share, the median and the mode, and drawing conclusions. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Put the data in order first. The median is the middle value, the mode is the most common value, and the mean is a fair share.
key_sub: Mean = total ÷ number of values. The mode is the value that appears most often, not the biggest number. In a stem-and-leaf plot, 3 | 4 means 34.
body_html:
Qualitative and quantitative data

Qualitative data is words or categories, such as favourite colours or ways to get to school. Quantitative data is numbers you count or measure, such as the number of pets or a height in centimetres. Data you collect yourself is primary data. Data someone else collected, such as on a website, is secondary data.

Kind of dataExamplesGood ways to show it
QualitativeFavourite sport, kind of pet, month of birthdayFrequency table, bar graph, multiple-bar graph
QuantitativeNumber of siblings, height, minutes of readingFrequency table, stem-and-leaf plot

Stem-and-leaf plots

A stem-and-leaf plot shows every number in a data set. The stem is the tens digit. The leaf is the ones digit. The leaves are written in order, so the data is already sorted.

Example 1

What are the median and the mode?

There are 9 leaves, so the median is the 5th value: 24, 27, 31, 35, 35. The leaf 5 appears twice on stem 3, so 35 is also the mode.

Answer: Median 35 laps, mode 35 laps

Multiple-bar graphs

A multiple-bar graph puts bars for two or more groups side by side, so you can compare them. The key shows which colour is which group. Like every graph, it needs a title, labels, a scale and a source.

Example 2

How many students chose apples in all?

4A: 8. 4B: 6. 8 + 6 = 14.

Answer: 14 students

Mean, median and mode

MeasureHow to find itWhat it tells you
MeanAdd all the values, then divide by how many there areThe fair share: what each would get if shared equally
MedianPut the values in order and take the middle oneThe middle of the data
ModeThe value that appears most often (there can be two, or none)The most common value

Think of the mean as levelling towers of cubes. Move cubes from tall towers to short towers until all the towers are the same height.

With an even number of values, the median is halfway between the two middle values: for 3, 5, 9, 11 it is (5 + 9) ÷ 2 = 7.

Example 3

Goals in 5 games: 4, 1, 3, 1, 6. Find the mean, the median and the mode.

Mean: 4 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 6 = 15, and 15 ÷ 5 = 3. Median: in order 1, 1, 3, 4, 6, so the middle is 3. Mode: 1 appears twice.

Answer: Mean 3, median 3, mode 1

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Finding the median without putting the values in orderOrder the values first, then take the middle
Giving the biggest number as the modeThe mode is the value that appears most often
Giving the frequency (how many times) as the modeThe mode is the value itself, not its count
Giving the total as the meanDivide the total by how many values there are
Reading 6 | 2 as 26The stem is the tens: 6 | 2 means 62
Reading the other group’s barCheck the key for the right colour

faq.q: What do Grade 4 students learn about data in the Ontario math curriculum?
faq.a: Grade 4 students tell qualitative from quantitative data, organize data in frequency tables and stem-and-leaf plots, read and make multiple-bar graphs, find the mean, median and mode, and draw conclusions from data.

faq.q: How do you explain the mean to a Grade 4 student?
faq.a: The mean is a fair share. Add all the values, then share the total equally: for 2, 6 and 4, the total is 12, and 12 ÷ 3 = 4.

faq.q: How do you read a stem-and-leaf plot?
faq.a: The stem is the tens digit and each leaf is a ones digit, so 4 | 2 7 means 42 and 47. Each leaf is one piece of data.

faq.q: What is the difference between qualitative and quantitative data?
faq.a: Qualitative data is words or categories, such as favourite colours. Quantitative data is numbers you count or measure, such as the number of pets or a height.

sets.title: Qualitative or quantitative data and frequency tables

items.q:
Is this data qualitative or quantitative?
Each student’s favourite colour
items.e: The answers are words, such as red or blue. Data in words or categories is qualitative.

items.q:
Is this data qualitative or quantitative?
The number of brothers and sisters each student has
items.e: The answers are numbers you count: 0, 1, 2, 3 … Number data is quantitative.

items.q:
Is this data qualitative or quantitative?
The height of each student in centimetres
items.e: Height is a number you measure, such as 136 cm. Number data is quantitative.

items.q:
Is this data qualitative or quantitative?
Each student’s favourite hockey team
items.e: The answers are team names, not numbers, so the data is qualitative.

items.q:
Is this data qualitative or quantitative?
How each student gets to school: walk, bus, car or bike
items.e: The answers are categories (walk, bus, car, bike), so the data is qualitative.

items.q:
Is this data qualitative or quantitative?
The time each student takes to run one lap of the track, in seconds
items.e: Time is a number you measure, such as 75 seconds, so the data is quantitative.

items.q:
Is this data qualitative or quantitative?
The kind of pet each student has
items.e: The answers are words such as dog, cat or fish, so the data is qualitative.

items.q:
Is this data qualitative or quantitative?
The number of books each student read in March
items.e: The answers are numbers you count, so the data is quantitative.

items.q:
Is this data qualitative or quantitative?
The temperature at recess each day, in °C
items.e: Temperature is a number you measure with a thermometer, so the data is quantitative.

items.q:
Is this data qualitative or quantitative?
The month of each student’s birthday
items.e: The answers are month names (January, February …). They are categories, so the data is qualitative.

items.q:
Is this data qualitative or quantitative?
The mass of each pumpkin at a Thanksgiving market, in kilograms
items.e: Mass is a number you measure on a scale, so the data is quantitative.

items.q:
Is this data qualitative or quantitative?
The flavour of ice cream each student likes best
items.e: The answers are flavours such as chocolate or maple, so the data is qualitative.

items.q:
Is this data qualitative or quantitative?
The number on each player’s hockey jersey
items.e: Jersey numbers only name the players, like labels. Adding them or finding their mean makes no sense, so they are qualitative, even though they look like numbers.

items.q: Which survey question gives quantitative data?
c: How many pets do you have?
items.e: “How many pets?” is answered with a number, so it gives quantitative data. The other questions are answered with words.

items.q: Which survey question gives qualitative data?
c: How many minutes do you read?
How many cousins do you have?
items.e: “What is your favourite season?” is answered with a word (winter, spring …), so it gives qualitative data. The other questions are answered with numbers.

items.q: How many students answered the survey?
items.e: Add the frequencies: 9 + 7 + 6 + 3 = 25 students. (4 is the number of rows, 9 is only the biggest row, and 22 leaves out Bike.)

items.q: How many more students walk than take the bus?
items.e: Walk 9, bus 7. 9 − 7 = 2 more students. (16 adds the two rows.)

items.q: What is the mode of this data?
items.e: The most common answer is 1 sibling: 9 students gave it. The mode is the value, 1, not the frequency, 9. (4 is the biggest value in the table.)

items.q: How many students have 2 or more siblings?
items.e: 2 or more means the rows 2, 3 and 4: 6 + 3 + 1 = 10 students. (6 is only the row for 2, and 19 counts 2 or fewer.)

items.q: Is this data qualitative or quantitative?
c: Qualitative: it is in a table
items.e: Each student answered with a number (0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 siblings), so the data is quantitative. A table or tally marks can show either kind of data.

items.q: In a stem-and-leaf plot, 3 | 7 means 37. What does 5 | 2 mean?
items.e: The stem is the tens digit and the leaf is the ones digit: 5 tens and 2 ones = 52. (25 swaps the digits, and 7 adds them.)

items.q: Which row of a stem-and-leaf plot shows 61, 64 and 68?
items.e: All three numbers have 6 tens, so the stem is 6. The leaves are the ones digits: 1, 4 and 8. (6 | 1 8 leaves out 64.)

items.q: A row of a stem-and-leaf plot is 4 | 0 3 3 7. Which values does it show?
items.e: Each leaf makes one value with the stem 4: 40, 43, 43, 47. The leaf 3 is written twice, so 43 appears twice. (40, 43, 47 drops the repeated leaf.)

items.q: Where does the value 30 go in a stem-and-leaf plot?
items.e: 30 is 3 tens and 0 ones, so it goes on stem 3 with a leaf of 0. Without the leaf 0, the value would be lost.

items.q: Data: 23, 18, 27, 15, 21, 18. Which is the row for stem 1?
items.e: The values with 1 ten are 18, 15 and 18. Their ones digits in order are 5, 8, 8. (1 | 5 8 drops one 18, and 1 | 8 5 8 is not in order.)

items.q: How many students are shown in this plot?
items.e: Each leaf is one student. Count the leaves: 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 0 + 1 = 15. (6 counts the stems, 5 counts the rows that have leaves, and 62 is the largest value.)

items.q: What is the longest time a student read?
items.e: The last row is 6 | 2, which means 62 minutes. (45 is the end of the row for 4, and 26 reads the digits the wrong way round.)

items.q: What is the shortest time a student read?
items.e: The first leaf on the first row: 1 | 2 means 12 minutes. (21 reads the digits the wrong way round.)

items.q: How many students read for 50 to 59 minutes?
items.e: The row for stem 5 has no leaves, so 0 students read for 50 to 59 minutes. (An empty row is not one student.)

items.q: What is the mode?
items.e: The leaf 5 appears three times on stem 1, so 15 appears most often. The mode is 15 minutes. (62 is the largest value, and 3 is how many times 15 appears.)

items.q: What is the median?
items.e: The leaves are already in order. 15 values, so the median is the 8th: 12, 15, 15, 15, 18, 21, 23, 26. (37 is halfway between 12 and 62, which is not the median, and 27 is the 9th value.)

items.q: How many students read for 30 minutes or more?
items.e: 30 or more: 30, 33, 36, 41, 45, 62. That is 6 students. (5 forgets 30, and 9 counts the students under 30.)

items.q: How many more students read for 10 to 19 minutes than for 40 to 49 minutes?
items.e: Row 1 has 5 leaves and row 4 has 2 leaves. 5 − 2 = 3 more students. (7 adds them.)

items.q: What is the median?
items.e: There are 13 values, so the median is the 7th: 38, 42, 45, 45, 45, 47, 51. (47 is the 6th and 53 is the 8th value.)

items.q: What is the mode?
items.e: 45 appears three times (the leaf 5 three times on stem 4), more than any other value. (64 is the largest value.)

items.q: How many students did more than 55 jumping jacks?
items.e: More than 55: 56, 58, 60, 62, 64. That is 5 students. (3 counts only the row for 6, and 7 counts everything from 50.)

items.q: How many students did fewer than 50 jumping jacks?
items.e: Fewer than 50: the rows for 3 and 4. 1 + 5 = 6 students. (5 counts only the row for 4, and 2 counts the rows, not the leaves.)

items.q: Mei did 48 jumping jacks. How does the row for 4 look after her value is added?
items.e: 48 has 4 tens and 8 ones, so the leaf 8 goes on stem 4, in order after 7. (4 | 2 5 7 8 also loses the repeated 5s.)

items.q: Which data set does this plot show?
items.e: Stem 3 with leaves 1 and 5 gives 31 and 35. Stem 4 with leaves 2, 8, 8 gives 42, 48 and 48. (13, 53 … read the digits the wrong way round, and 31, 35, 42, 48 drops the repeated 48.)

items.q: Why are the leaves in a stem-and-leaf plot written in order from least to greatest?
c: The median and mode are easy to find
items.e: When the leaves are in order, the whole data set is in order. You can count to the middle value for the median and see repeated leaves for the mode.

items.q: Which graph is best for comparing the favourite fruits of two classes?
items.e: A multiple-bar graph puts a bar for each class side by side for each fruit, so the two classes are easy to compare. A stem-and-leaf plot is for number data, not fruits.

items.q: What does the key on a multiple-bar graph tell you?
c: The total of all the bars
items.e: The key shows the colour for each group, such as green for 4A and orange for 4B. The source tells where the data came from.

items.q: Which part of a graph tells where the data came from?
items.e: The source names where the data came from, such as “Source: class survey” or a website.

items.q: Which data is best shown in a stem-and-leaf plot?
items.e: A stem-and-leaf plot shows number data, such as scores from 0 to 100. Colours, pets and votes for categories are better in a bar graph.

items.q: How many books did 4B read in November?
items.e: Find the orange 4B bar for Nov. It reaches the line for 36. (32 is the green 4A bar, and 9 counts the grid spaces instead of reading the scale, which counts by 4s.)

items.q: In which month did both classes read the same number of books?
items.e: In January both bars reach 24, so both classes read 24 books.

items.q: In which month did 4A read more books than 4B?
items.e: Only in October is the green 4A bar taller: 28 books for 4A and 20 for 4B.

items.q: In December, how many more books did 4B read than 4A?
items.e: December: 4B read 24 and 4A read 12. 24 − 12 = 12 more books. (36 adds the bars, and 8 is the difference in October.)

items.q: How many books did 4A read in all four months?
items.e: Add the green bars: 28 + 32 + 12 + 24 = 96 books. (104 adds the orange 4B bars, and 32 is only the tallest green bar.)

items.q: What does the scale on this graph count by?
items.e: The numbers on the scale are 0, 4, 8, 12 … so each line is 4 more than the one below it.

items.q: How many Grade 5 students chose sledding?
items.e: Find the orange Grade 5 bar for sledding. It ends one line above 10, so it shows 11. (8 is the green Grade 4 bar.)

items.q: Which activities got more votes from Grade 5 than from Grade 4?
items.e: Skiing: Grade 5 has 9 and Grade 4 has 5. Sledding: Grade 5 has 11 and Grade 4 has 8. For hockey and skating, the Grade 4 bar is taller.

items.q: How many students chose skating in all?
items.e: Add both skating bars: 9 + 6 = 15 students. (3 is the difference between the bars.)

items.q: How many more Grade 4 students than Grade 5 students chose hockey?
items.e: Hockey: Grade 4 has 12 and Grade 5 has 10. 12 − 10 = 2 more students. (22 adds the two bars.)

items.q: Which activity was the favourite in Grade 4?
items.e: The tallest green bar is hockey, with 12 votes. (Sledding is the favourite in Grade 5.)

items.q: How many Grade 4 students voted?
items.e: Add the green bars: 12 + 9 + 5 + 8 = 34. (36 adds the orange Grade 5 bars, and 70 adds both grades.)

items.q: Which activity got the most votes from both grades together?
items.e: Add the two bars for each activity: hockey 22, skating 15, skiing 14, sledding 19. Hockey has the most. (12 and 11 are single bars.)

items.q: For which activity is the difference between the two grades the greatest?
items.e: Differences: hockey 12 − 10 = 2, skating 9 − 6 = 3, skiing 9 − 5 = 4, sledding 11 − 8 = 3. Skiing has the greatest difference, even though its bars are not the tallest.

items.q: Why use one multiple-bar graph instead of two separate bar graphs for two classes?
c: Side-by-side bars are easy to compare
It does not need a scale
It does not need a key
items.e: In a multiple-bar graph the bars for both classes stand next to each other, so you can see at once which is taller. It still needs a scale and a key.

items.q: Amira makes a multiple-bar graph of goals scored by two ringette teams in 5 games. What must her graph have?
c: Title, labels, scale, key and source
items.e: Every graph needs a title, labels on the axes, a scale and a source. A multiple-bar graph also needs a key to show which colour is which team.

items.q:
Goals scored by a hockey team in 8 games:
3, 6, 2, 4, 4, 5, 4, 1
What is the mode?
items.e: The mode is the value that appears most often. 4 appears 3 times, so the mode is 4 goals. (6 is the biggest value, 3 is how many times 4 appears, and 8 is the number of games.)

items.q:
Laps skated by 7 students:
7, 9, 7, 8, 10, 9, 6
What is the mode?
items.e: 7 appears twice and 9 appears twice. Every other value appears once. So there are two modes: 7 and 9. (10 is the biggest value.)

items.q:
Quiz scores out of 15:
12, 8, 15, 10, 9
What is the mode?
items.e: Each score appears only once, so no value appears most often. There is no mode. (15 is the highest score, 5 is how many scores there are, and 10 is the median.)

items.q:
Favourite fruits of 7 students:
apple, banana, apple, orange, grape, apple, banana
What is the mode?
items.e: Apple appears 3 times, more than any other fruit, so the mode is apple. (3 is how many times it appears, not the mode.)

items.q:
Minutes 5 students spent on homework:
9, 4, 12, 7, 5
What is the median?
items.e: Put the values in order first: 4, 5, 7, 9, 12. The middle value is 7. (12 is the middle of the list before it was put in order, and 8 is halfway between 4 and 12.)

items.q:
Ages of 7 people at a skating party:
15, 22, 18, 30, 18, 25, 20
What is the median?
items.e: In order: 15, 18, 18, 20, 22, 25, 30. The middle (4th) value is 20. (30 is the middle of the unordered list, and 18 is the mode.)

items.q:
Lengths swum by 4 students:
3, 11, 9, 5
What is the median?
items.e: In order: 3, 5, 9, 11. There are two middle values, 5 and 9. The median is halfway between them: (5 + 9) ÷ 2 = 7. (10 uses 11 and 9 from the unordered list, and 14 forgets to divide by 2.)

items.q: Move cubes until all 5 towers are the same height. How tall is each tower? (This is the mean.)
items.e: There are 3 + 7 + 5 + 1 + 4 = 20 cubes. Shared fairly among 5 towers: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 cubes each. (20 is the total, 7 is the tallest tower, and 5 is the number of towers.)

items.q: What is the mean height of these towers?
items.e: Total: 2 + 8 + 5 = 15 cubes. Shared among 3 towers: 15 ÷ 3 = 5. (15 is the total, 8 is the tallest tower, and 3 is the number of towers.)

items.q: To make the towers even, how many cubes move from tower B to tower A?
items.e: The mean is 5. Tower B has 8, which is 3 too many. Tower A has 2, which is 3 too few. Move 3 cubes from B to A: then A, B and C all have 5. (6 is the difference between B and A.)

items.q:
Points scored by Priya in 4 basketball games:
2, 9, 5, 8
What is the mean?
items.e: Add: 2 + 9 + 5 + 8 = 24. There are 4 games: 24 ÷ 4 = 6 points. (24 is the total, 8 divides by 3, and 9 is the highest score.)

items.q:
Centimetres of snow that fell each day for 5 days:
0, 6, 3, 0, 6
What is the mean?
items.e: Add: 0 + 6 + 3 + 0 + 6 = 15. There are 5 days, including the 2 days with 0 cm: 15 ÷ 5 = 3 cm. (5 leaves out the zeros and divides by 3.)

items.q: Four friends picked 36 apples at an orchard. They share them equally. How many apples does each friend get? (This is the mean.)
items.e: Share 36 equally among 4: 36 ÷ 4 = 9 apples each. (32 subtracts, 40 adds and 144 multiplies.)

items.q: Which measure is the middle value when the data is in order?
items.e: The median is the middle value of the ordered data. The mode is the most common value, and the mean is the fair share.

items.q: Students named their favourite colours. Which measure can you find for this data?
items.e: Colours are qualitative: you cannot add them or put them in number order. You can only find the colour that appears most often, the mode.

items.q: Liam says the mode of 2, 3, 3, 9 is 9 because 9 is the biggest number. Who is right?
items.e: The mode is the value that appears most often, not the biggest value. 3 appears twice, so the mode is 3. (2 is how many times 3 appears.)

items.q: Hana says the median of 8, 2, 5 is 2 because 2 is in the middle of the list. What is right?
items.e: Always put the values in order before you find the middle. In order: 2, 5, 8. The middle value is 5.

items.q:
Ava’s spelling test scores out of 20:
19, 20, 14, 17, 20
What is the mean?
items.e: Add: 19 + 20 + 14 + 17 + 20 = 90. There are 5 tests: 90 ÷ 5 = 18. (90 is the total, 20 is the mode, and 19 is the median.)

items.q: The mean of 3 numbers is 6. Two of the numbers are 4 and 5. What is the third number?
items.e: A mean of 6 for 3 numbers means the total is 3 × 6 = 18. 4 + 5 = 9, and 18 − 9 = 9. Check: (4 + 5 + 9) ÷ 3 = 6. (15 adds 6, 4 and 5, and 3 uses 2 × 6 = 12 instead of 18.)

items.q: Which data set has a mean of 5, a median of 5 and a mode of 5?
items.e: 3, 5, 5, 7: total 20, and 20 ÷ 4 = 5. Middle values 5 and 5, so the median is 5. 5 appears twice, so the mode is 5. (5, 5, 6, 8 has a mean of 6, 1, 5, 9 has no mode, and 4, 5, 6, 6 has a mode of 6.)

items.q: Noah asks everyone in his class how they get to school. What kind of data does he collect?
c: Primary: it is on a website
items.e: Data you collect yourself, with a survey or by measuring, is primary data.

items.q: Maya finds the number of visitors to Algonquin Park last summer on a government website. What kind of data is this?
c: Primary: it is about a park
items.e: Maya did not count the visitors herself. Data that someone else collected is secondary data.

items.q:
Cans collected for the food drive: Liam 14, Zoe 9, Arjun 12, Mei 6, Owen 9.
What is the mean number of cans?
items.e: Add: 14 + 9 + 12 + 6 + 9 = 50. There are 5 students: 50 ÷ 5 = 10 cans. (50 is the total, 9 is the median and the mode, and 14 is the most.)

items.q:
Cans collected for the food drive: Liam 14, Zoe 9, Arjun 12, Mei 6, Owen 9.
Who collected more cans than the mean?
items.e: The mean is 50 ÷ 5 = 10. Liam (14) and Arjun (12) collected more than 10. Zoe and Owen collected 9, which is less.

items.q: Minutes 5 friends take to walk to school: 8, 10, 9, 11, 42. Which number best describes a typical time?
items.e: 42 is far from the other times. It pulls the mean up to 80 ÷ 5 = 16, which is more than 4 of the 5 times. The median, 10, is in the middle of the usual times.

items.q: Liam says, “Most of the class chose pepperoni.” Is this supported?
c: No: 9 of 26 is less than half
items.e: Pepperoni is the mode, but “most” means more than half. There are 9 + 7 + 6 + 4 = 26 votes. Half of 26 is 13, and only 9 chose pepperoni.

items.q: The class can order two kinds of pizza for a party. Which two should they choose?
items.e: Choose the two kinds with the most votes: pepperoni (9) and cheese (7).

items.q: 4A says, “We read more books than 4B every month.” Is this true?
c: No: 4B read more in Nov and Dec
items.e: 4A read more only in October. In November and December the orange 4B bars are taller, and in January the classes read the same.

items.q: Owen thinks most Grade 4 students like skating best. Does the data support his idea?
c: No: skiing got the most votes
Yes: skating is popular in Grade 5
No: hockey got more Grade 4 votes
items.e: In Grade 4, hockey got 12 votes and skating got 9. The data shows his idea is not right.

items.q: Which conclusion is supported by the graph?
c: More Grade 5 students chose sledding than hockey
More Grade 4 students than Grade 5 students chose skiing
items.e: Grade 5: sledding 11, hockey 10, so sledding has more. Grade 4 chose skiing only 5 times (Grade 5: 9), 6 Grade 5 students chose skating, and Grade 4 liked hockey best.

items.q: To find the favourite sport of all Grade 4 students, Kai asks only the players on his hockey team. What is the problem?
c: His team probably likes hockey best
items.e: Players on a hockey team are likely to choose hockey. To be fair, Kai should ask students from all Grade 4 classes.

items.q: Ava asks 3 friends if they like broccoli. All 3 say yes. She says, “Everyone in our school likes broccoli.” Why is this a weak conclusion?
c: 3 out of 3 is less than half
3 people are too few to ask
items.e: 3 friends cannot speak for a whole school. A different group could give a very different answer.

items.q: Litres of maple syrup a sugar bush made each week in spring: 12, 15, 9, 15, 14. What is the mean?
items.e: Add: 12 + 15 + 9 + 15 + 14 = 65. There are 5 weeks: 65 ÷ 5 = 13 L. (65 is the total, 15 is the mode, and 14 is the median.)

items.q: Three friends picked 7, 11 and 9 baskets of apples. They share all the baskets equally. How many baskets does each friend get?
items.e: Total: 7 + 11 + 9 = 27 baskets. Shared among 3: 27 ÷ 3 = 9 baskets each. This fair share is the mean. (27 is the total, and 4 is 11 − 7.)

items.q: Sizes of skates rented at a rink one Saturday: 4, 5, 5, 6, 3, 5, 7, 4, 5. Which size should the rink keep the most of?
items.e: Size 5 was rented 4 times, more than any other size. The mode tells the rink which size is needed most.

items.q: The coach says, “More than half of the students did 50 or more jumping jacks.” Is this supported?
items.e: 50 or more: the rows for 5 and 6. 4 + 3 = 7 students. Half of 13 is 6 and a half, and 7 is more, so the claim is supported. (3 counts only the row for 6.)

items.q:
Goals scored by two ringette teams in 4 games:
Lightning: 3, 5, 2, 6
Storm: 4, 4, 5, 3
Which statement is true?
c: The Lightning have the higher mean
The Storm have the higher mean
The Lightning scored more goals in all
Both teams have a mean of 4 goals
items.e: Lightning: 3 + 5 + 2 + 6 = 16, and 16 ÷ 4 = 4. Storm: 4 + 4 + 5 + 3 = 16, and 16 ÷ 4 = 4. One big game (6 goals) does not give the Lightning a higher mean.

items.q: Heights of 4 sunflowers in a school garden (cm): 166, 148, 172, 160. What is the median height?
items.e: In order: 148, 160, 166, 172. The two middle values are 160 and 166: (160 + 166) ÷ 2 = 326 ÷ 2 = 163 cm. (160 is halfway between 148 and 172 from the unordered list, and 326 forgets to divide by 2.)

items.q: Hours Kai slept each night for a week: 9, 10, 9, 8, 9, 10, 8. Which statement is true?
c: Mean, median and mode are all 9
items.e: Mean: 63 ÷ 7 = 9. In order: 8, 8, 9, 9, 9, 10, 10, so the median is 9. 9 appears 3 times, so the mode is 9. (63 is the total, not the mean.)

items.q: The 4 Grade 4 classes raised $480 for the Terry Fox Run. What is the mean amount raised per class?
items.e: Share $480 equally among 4 classes: 480 ÷ 4 = 120, so $120 per class. ($476 subtracts 4, $484 adds 4, and $1920 multiplies by 4.)
